description: We are a group of science-lovers who have a desire of learning, creating, and coding.
summary: Our project is a blend of science and innovation, combining aspects of both a universe simulator and a mission sandbox. From exploring our Solar System's planets, to learning how to make a successful satellite, HELIO-FORGE covers them all. We teach important skills needed for successful coordination in day-to-day life, including resource management and design planning.
details:
HELIO-FORGE

What does the project do?

HELIO-FORGE is an educational space mission design game combined with an interactive Solar System and galaxy explorer. It lets users think like mission designers: start with a scientific question, build a spacecraft around it, and see how engineering decisions affect the science returned to Earth.

In the Mission Lab, players choose an objective—tracking wildfires, watching coastal waters, or measuring the atmosphere—and select an orbit, instrument, spacecraft bus, power system, communications, ground network, launch service and mission duration. The game shows how those choices affect mass, cost, power and data return. During the simulated mission, players respond to three events and then receive a debrief with a flight log, charts and engineering feedback. They can improve their design, compare fictional campaign conditions, save progress locally or share a design link.

The Explore experience connects that mission to a wider view of space. Users can navigate the Solar System, investigate nearby stars, view a schematic Milky Way and explore six curated exoplanet systems. An Earth profile can also pass a science objective into the Mission Lab.

Benefits and intended impact

HELIO-FORGE makes complex mission-design concepts approachable through experimentation. Instead of only reading about spacecraft, users can see why an instrument needs enough power, why storage and downlink matter, and why a more capable design must still fit its budget and launch capacity.

The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about Earth science, space exploration and engineering—especially among students and people without a technical background. By showing that every design involves trade-offs, the project aims to help users understand both what space missions make possible and how much planning goes into achieving their goals.

Tools and technologies

We developed HELIO-FORGE as a browser-based application using JavaScript, React, HTML and CSS, with Three.js for interactive 3D graphics and Vite for development and builds. A Node.js and Express backend provides routes for external data services, and the project includes a Vercel deployment adapter.

The project draws on NASA resources for mission-design context and Earth imagery, as well as astronomical catalogue data including HYG and a selected Gaia DR3 sample. It uses Astronomy Engine for parts of the Solar System calculations. The mission concept artwork includes AI-generated images, and development was supported by Arena.ai.

No special hardware is required to use the application beyond a compatible device and modern browser. Where WebGL is unavailable, the explorers offer interactive 2D alternatives, while the mission visualization has a schematic fallback.

What makes it creative?

HELIO-FORGE combines a hands-on engineering game with a journey through the cosmos. Rather than treating spacecraft design as a static checklist, it turns each mission into a story: a player chooses a question, makes compromises, responds to events and learns from the result.

The campaign comparison lets users ask “what if?” by testing the same spacecraft and decisions under different fictional conditions. The connection between Earth exploration and the Mission Lab also helps bridge the gap between seeing a world and considering how a spacecraft might study it.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: The mission model is educational and deterministic, not a validated flight-design tool. Component values and campaign events are illustrative, and conceptual artwork is labelled as such.
  • Accessibility: We included keyboard-accessible controls, mobile layouts, reduced-motion support and 2D fallbacks so the experience is not dependent on 3D graphics.
  • Clarity: Preflight checks, explanations, charts and a mission debrief help users understand why a design performed as it did, not just see a score.
  • Performance: Graphics are loaded and scaled with device capabilities in mind, while catalogues and visual detail have practical limits.
  • Privacy and reliability: Mission progress is saved locally when browser storage is available; shared links contain design choices rather than flight decisions or reports.
  • Scope and limitations: The galaxy and planetary views are incomplete and often schematic. Live NASA/JPL services and the Vercel deployment still require verification in their target environment.
